01.note: A man rented his donkey to another and told him not to take the path of Nehar Pekod, where there was water, but the dry path of Neresh. The renter took the Nehar Pekod path anyway and the donkey died. When he came back he admitted going that way but claimed there had been no water. Rava said his claim is believed, since if he wanted to lie he could have said he took the Neresh path; Abaye answered that this 'why would he lie' reasoning is not used where witnesses can settle the matter.
01.why: Rabbi Ile'a has ruled that a priest is believed when he says a blemish on his firstborn animal happened by accident. Mar bar Rav Ashi raises the donkey case to challenge this; the Gemara answers that there the water was certain, while here the priest's tampering is only a suspicion.

people.name: Mar bar Rav Ashi
people.about: The Sage who raises this earlier case as an objection to the ruling under discussion.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Rules that the renter is believed, since he could have told an easier lie.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Disputes Rava: the 'why would he lie' argument does not apply where witnesses are available.

terms.meaning: A rule of evidence: if a person could have won with a simpler, more convenient claim but made a less convenient one instead, his claim is believed, since a liar would have chosen the easier story.

02.note: Rabbi Tzadok, a priest, had a firstborn animal whose lip split while it ate barley from a wicker basket. He asked Rabbi Yehoshua whether a learned priest is treated differently from an ignorant one in such a case, and was told yes. Rabban Gamliel told him no, and when the scholars gathered in the study hall the question was asked publicly. Rabbi Yehoshua now said no; Rabban Gamliel ordered him to stand while witnesses testified against him, and Rabbi Yehoshua admitted that the living cannot contradict the living. Rabban Gamliel went on lecturing while Rabbi Yehoshua stood, until the crowd murmured and told Hutzpit, the one relaying the lecture, to stop, and he stopped.
02.why: The discussion is about whether a priest is believed that a blemish on his own firstborn animal was not caused on purpose. Rabbi Tzadok's question, whether a learned priest is trusted more than an ignorant one, is exactly that issue, and the mishna that follows continues it.

people.name: Rabbi Tzadok
people.about: A learned priest whose firstborn animal was blemished; he brings the question to both Sages.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua
people.about: Tells Rabbi Tzadok privately that a learned priest is treated differently, then says otherwise in public.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: The Nasi, head of the academy; he rules otherwise and makes Rabbi Yehoshua stand during his lecture.

people.name: Hutzpit
people.about: The disseminator who repeated Rabban Gamliel's lecture aloud to the crowd; the people tell him to stop.

terms.meaning: The firstborn male of a cow, sheep or goat belongs to a priest and is holy. It may be eaten as ordinary meat only if it has a permanent blemish, so priests were suspected of causing blemishes on purpose.
A learned and careful person, trusted to keep the laws; the opposite of an ignoramus.
The president of the Sages' council and head of the academy.
A speaker who repeated a Sage's lecture in a loud voice so the whole assembly could hear it.

03.note: Rafram, in Pumbedita, gave his firstborn animal to a priest unblemished, and the priest went and caused a blemish in it. One day, when Rafram's eyes were afflicted, the priest brought the animal before him to be declared fit, saying an Israelite had given it to him already blemished. Rafram forced his eyes open, recognized the animal, and said to him: Is it not I who gave this to you?
03.why: Rav ruled that a priest is believed when he says an Israelite gave him a firstborn already blemished, and Pumbedita taught it that way. The Gemara adds that Rafram still kept trusting other priests: only this one was so brazen.

people.name: Rafram
people.about: A Sage in Pumbedita who examined firstborn animals; he had given this animal to the priest himself.

terms.meaning: The firstborn male of a cow, sheep or goat is given to a priest and is holy. He may eat it as ordinary meat only once an expert confirms a permanent blemish, so priests were suspected of causing blemishes.

04.note: Rabbi Yohanan ben Elazar recalled an elder in his neighborhood, Rabbi Shimon ben Yosei Lakonya, whom he had never passed in front of. Once he did, and the elder said: Sit, my son, sit. He taught him that the 'snail' growth in a firstborn's eye is a permanent blemish, allowing the animal to be slaughtered, and that it is the same as the 'snake' the Sages mention. He added that although a person may not judge blemishes for himself, a teacher may teach his students the law and the students may then rule for him.
04.why: The mishna lists a 'snail' and a 'snake' among eye blemishes, and the Sages asked whether these are one blemish or two. This account answers that they are the same. The Gemara then asks how a ruling made for the elder's own benefit could be trusted.

people.name: Rabba bar bar Hana
people.about: Passes on the account he heard from Rabbi Yohanan ben Elazar.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan ben Elazar
people.about: The narrator, who once passed before the elder and was taught by him.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon ben Yosei Lakonya
people.about: An elder in Rabbi Yohanan ben Elazar's neighborhood who teaches him about the eye blemish.

terms.meaning: A lasting physical defect that disqualifies a firstborn animal from the altar, so it may be slaughtered and eaten as ordinary meat.
The firstborn male of a cow, sheep or goat, which is holy and belongs to a priest.

05.note: In Piran of Beit Menahem, a firstborn animal seemed to have only one testicle. Someone mashed its sac to see whether a second one would come out, and none did. The animal was slaughtered, and the testicle was found attached to the loins. Rabbi Akiva permitted the meat, and Rabbi Yohanan ben Nuri prohibited it.
05.why: The mishna lists a missing testicle as a blemish and gives Rabbi Akiva's test: mash the sac and see if one emerges. This teaching adds the place of the incident; the two Sages' sharp exchange over it follows.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei
people.about: Reports the incident in a baraita.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: Permitted the animal's meat, since the testicle had not emerged when tested.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan ben Nuri
people.about: Prohibited the animal's meat.

terms.meaning: The firstborn male of a cow, sheep or goat is holy and may be eaten as ordinary meat only if it has a blemish; without one it is a sacrifice.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the core law code the Gemara discusses.

06.note: A teaching listed the tzime'ah among the blemishes that keep a priest from serving in the Temple, but the Sages did not know what the word meant. They heard an Arab calling out, 'Who wants a tzime'ah?', and it turned out to be a long-eared goat.
06.why: The mishna lists ear blemishes, the tzomem and the tzome'a, that disqualify a priest, and a baraita adds the tzime'ah. The overheard Arab is how the Sages learned what that word means.

terms.meaning: A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the core law code the Gemara discusses.
An unusual word for a bodily blemish; from the Arab's use, the Sages learned it describes long ears, as on a long-eared goat.

07.note: Shmuel needed to urinate on the Shabbat when crowds gathered to hear the laws of the coming Festival, and people spread a sheet around him for privacy. His father said he would give him four hundred dinars to go and undo the impression this had made. You can have a sheet held up, he said, but should someone who cannot endanger himself by holding back?
07.why: Rabbi Abba has just taught that Torah scholars may urinate in public, since holding back harms the body, and a baraita tells of a man whose belly swelled from holding back. Shmuel's father wants that permission seen to apply to everyone, not only those who can arrange privacy.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: A Sage who needed to relieve himself during a public gathering and was screened with a sheet.

people.name: his father
people.about: Shmuel's father, who offers him money to correct the example he set.

terms.meaning: One of the pilgrimage holidays (Passover, Shavuot, Sukkot). On the Shabbat before one, crowds came to hear its laws taught.
A silver coin; four hundred was a very large sum.

08.note: Mar bar Rav Ashi needed to urinate while crossing the beams of a bridge, and he did. People told him his mother-in-law was coming. He told them he would have done it even in her ear.
08.why: The Gemara has ruled that one may urinate in public rather than hold back and endanger one's health; it follows Shmuel's story with this one, and goes on to explain the harm holding back can do.

people.name: Mar bar Rav Ashi
people.about: A Sage who relieves himself on a bridge and is not deterred when told his mother-in-law is approaching.

09.note: The students of Rabbi Yishmael boiled the body of a prostitute whom the king had sentenced to death by burning, to separate the flesh from the bones. They counted and found 252 limbs, more than the 248 the Sages taught. They were told, by Shmuel according to the English translation: Perhaps you examined a woman, for Scripture added to her two hinges and two doors.
09.why: The discussion concerns how many bones make up a majority of a human body for the laws of corpse impurity, based on 248 limbs. The story shows a woman's body counted with four more, and the Gemara then uses it against Rabbi Akiva, who says she also has a 'key'.

people.name: Rabbi Yishmael
people.about: The Sage whose students carried out the examination.

terms.meaning: Here, a bone with flesh and sinew on it. The Sages counted 248 in the human body.
The Sages' figurative names, drawn from verses about childbirth, for parts of a woman's body involved in giving birth, which they counted as extra limbs.

10.note: Rabbi Yehuda reported that a man with six fingers on each hand and six toes on each foot, twenty-four in all, came before Rabbi Tarfon, who said to him: May those like you increase among the Jewish people! Rabbi Yosei objected that this proves nothing: what Rabbi Tarfon really said was, May the mamzerim and Gibeonites be like you, so that they decrease from the Jewish people.
10.why: The mishna records a dispute: Rabbi Yehuda says a priest with extra fingers and toes may serve, the Rabbis say he may not. Rabbi Yehuda brings Rabbi Tarfon's words as a sign that extra digits are no blemish; Rabbi Yosei turns the same words into an insult.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: Tells the story as proof that extra fingers and toes are not a blemish.

people.name: Rabbi Tarfon
people.about: The Sage before whom the man with twenty-four digits came.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei
people.about: Disputes Rabbi Yehuda's version of what Rabbi Tarfon said.

terms.meaning: Children of a forbidden union, such as adultery, who are restricted in whom they may marry.
Descendants of the Gibeonites who joined Israel in Joshua's time; they too were restricted from marrying into ordinary Jewish families.

11.note: Rav Ashi sent seventeen dinars to Rav Aha, son of Ravina, a priest, to redeem a firstborn son, with a message: let the Master send back the extra third of a dinar included in the sum. Rav Aha sent back: let the Master send me the other three dinars the Sages added to the coin.
11.why: The Gemara has just reconciled two values of the Torah's shekel by explaining that the Sages later raised its value by a sixth. The two letters show the gap: by the old value seventeen dinars was slightly too much, by the raised value it was three short.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: Sends money for redeeming a firstborn son and asks for change.

people.name: Rav Aha, son of Ravina
people.about: The priest who received the money and replied that more was owed.

terms.meaning: A father pays a priest five sela, Torah-era silver coins, to redeem his firstborn son, as the Torah commands.
A silver coin; the value of the Torah's sela was reckoned in dinars, and the Sages raised it.

12.note: Hanan the wicked struck a man, and the man came before Rav Huna, who ordered Hanan to give him half a dinar. Hanan had only a worn dinar that was no longer in circulation. So he struck the man a second time and gave him the whole dinar.
12.why: Rav Asi has just taught that sums fixed by the Sages are in cheaper provincial coin, so the one-sela fine for an insulting blow is only half a dinar. Rav Huna's ruling applies that small fine, which Hanan treats as a price.

people.name: Hanan the wicked
people.about: A man who struck another, and struck him again to use up a whole coin.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: The judge who fined Hanan half a dinar.

terms.meaning: A silver coin. The fine for an insulting slap was a small 'sela' in local coin, worth half a dinar.

13.note: Rabbi Hanina, a priest, used to take the money for redeeming a firstborn son and give it back. Once he saw that a father who had paid him kept walking back and forth in front of him, hinting that he wanted it returned. Rabbi Hanina said: you never fully meant to give it. That is a bad thing, and therefore his son is not redeemed.
13.why: A baraita has just ruled that if the priest returns the redemption money the father has still fulfilled his duty, and Rabbi Tarfon did this regularly. This story shows the limit: the father must truly give the money.

people.name: Rabbi Hanina
people.about: A priest who would return the redemption money he received.

terms.meaning: A father pays a priest five silver coins to redeem his firstborn son, as the Torah commands.

14.note: Rabbi Yishmael ben Satriel of Arkat Leveina testified before Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi that in his place, when a mother animal died, they flayed her and dressed the living newborn in her skin. Rabbi said this revealed the reason for the mishna's ruling. He also reported lettuce with 600,000 leaves in its core, a fallen cedar so wide sixteen wagons drove along it side by side, and a bar yokhani egg that fell, drowned sixty cities and broke three hundred cedars. The Gemara asks how that bird could drop an egg when it lays on the ground; Rav Ashi said the egg was unfertilized.
14.why: The Gemara has just cited Rabbi Yehoshua: a newborn whose mother died is not an 'orphan' if her hide is there, which matters for tithing animals. The flaying custom explains why, since the hide stands in for the mother.

people.name: Rabbi Yishmael ben Satriel
people.about: A man from Arkat Leveina who reports the customs and wonders of his home before Rabbi.

people.name: Rabbi
people.about: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, before whom the testimony is given; he says it explains the mishna.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: Explains why the egg fell: it was unfertilized.

terms.meaning: Here, a newborn animal whose mother died. Such an animal is excluded from the animal tithe unless the mother's hide is present.
A legendary giant bird, which the Sages identified with a bird described in the book of Job.

15.note: Sha'azrak, an Arab merchant, donated a lamp to Rav Yehuda's synagogue. Rahava put it to a different use, and Rava was angry. Some say Rava changed it and Rahava was angry; others say the attendants of Pumbedita changed it, and both Rahava and Rabba were angry.
15.why: Rabbi Yohanan has ruled that a gentile's gift to a synagogue may not be put to another use while people still remember him, since he would protest. The Gemara then explains both sides: Sha'azrak seldom came to town, but sometimes he did.

people.name: Sha'azrak
people.about: An Arab merchant who donated a lamp to the synagogue.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: The Sage whose synagogue received the lamp.

people.name: Rahava
people.about: In one version changed the lamp's use; in the others was angry it was changed.

people.name: Rava
people.about: In one version was angry at the change; in another made it himself.

people.name: Rabba
people.about: In the third version, angry at the attendants who changed it.

terms.meaning: Communal officials who managed synagogue and charity matters.

16.note: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi once made nine months of the year 29-day months, yet the new moon still appeared on time. Astonished, he asked how this could be. His son Rabbi Shimon suggested that the previous year was a leap year with a 30-day added month, and two of its months had been lengthened to 30 days. The three short months this year balanced the three long ones last year, putting the moon back in place. Rabbi said to him: Lamp of Israel! So it was.
16.why: The Gemara is asking how many 30-day months a year may have, and says Rabbi held like Rav Huna that there may be more than usual. This incident is its proof.

people.name: Rabbi
people.about: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, who set the calendar that year and was puzzled by the result.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon, son of Rabbi
people.about: His son, who works out the explanation.

terms.meaning: Jewish months follow the moon and last either 30 days (full) or 29 days (deficient). The court decided which, to keep the calendar in step with the new moon.
A year with a thirteenth month added, to keep the lunar calendar in step with the seasons.

17.note: The Temple had an ancient reed flute, smooth and thin, from the days of Moses. A king ordered it plated with gold, and its sound lost its sweetness; when the plating was removed, the sound returned. The Temple also had a copper cymbal with a pleasant sound. When it was damaged, the Sages brought craftsmen from Alexandria in Egypt to repair it, but it no longer sounded as sweet; when the repair was removed, the old sound came back.
17.why: The mishna says the Temple flute was made of reed, not copper, because reed sounds sweeter, and the Gemara has just tied the word for flute to sweetness. This teaching backs that up, and goes on to a mortar with the same fate.

terms.meaning: A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the core law code the Gemara discusses.

18.note: The Temple had a copper mortar from the days of Moses, used to blend the spices for the incense. When it was damaged, craftsmen were brought from Alexandria in Egypt to repair it, but afterward it did not blend the spices as well. When the repair was removed, it worked as well as before.
18.why: This is one of a set of Temple traditions, following the flute and the cymbal, about ancient vessels that worked worse when improved. The teaching goes on to say the mortar and cymbal were left over from the First Temple and could not be properly repaired.

terms.meaning: A blend of spices burned daily in the Temple; the spices had to be ground and mixed precisely.

19.note: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel taught that the Siloam pool once gushed water through an opening the size of a small coin. A king ordered the opening widened so more water would flow, but the flow shrank. When they narrowed it again, the water gushed as before. He tied this to the verse: Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom, nor the mighty man in his might.
19.why: The Gemara has been collecting traditions about Temple objects, like the flute, cymbal and mortar, that got worse when people tried to improve them. This one adds a water source, and is followed by more of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's sayings about the Temple.

people.name: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
people.about: The Sage who teaches this tradition about the Siloam pool.

terms.meaning: A spring-fed pool in Jerusalem.
A small coin, used here as a measure of the opening's width.

20.note: Rabbi Yehoshua bar Hananya, a Levite, went to help Rabbi Yohanan ben Gudgeda, also a Levite, close the Temple doors. Rabbi Yohanan ben Gudgeda said to him: My son, go back, for you are one of the singers, not one of the gatekeepers.
20.why: Abaye says a Levite singer who serves as a gatekeeper is liable to death, while a baraita calls it only a prohibition. The Gemara first says this incident shows the Sages disagreed, then suggests both agree and differ only on whether a singer may even help.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua bar Hananya
people.about: A Levite of the singers who tried to help close the Temple doors.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan ben Gudgeda
people.about: A Levite gatekeeper who sent him back.

terms.meaning: Members of the tribe of Levi who served in the Temple below the priests; some were assigned as singers, others as gatekeepers, and each group kept to its own task.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the core law code the Gemara discusses.
